claim: Plasmodium falciparum remains one of the most common causes of malaria and childhood mortality in Africa.
source: Plasmodium falciparum remains one of the most common causes of malaria and childhood mortality in Africa despite significant efforts to eradicate the disease (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2022 report

claim: The World Health Organization estimated 247 million cases of malaria and 619,000 fatalities in 2021 alone.
source: The latest report by the World Health Organization estimated 247 million cases of malaria and 619,000 fatalities in 2021 alone, with the vast majority of deaths occurring in Africa (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2022 report

claim: The vast majority of malaria deaths in 2021 occurred in Africa.
source: The latest report by the World Health Organization estimated 247 million cases of malaria and 619,000 fatalities in 2021 alone, with the vast majority of deaths occurring in Africa (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2022 report

claim: The mainstay of malaria diagnosis across Africa is rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) rather than microscopy.
source: The mainstay of malaria diagnosis across Africa is no longer microscopy but rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) due to their simplicity and speed.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about diagnostic practices in Africa

claim: RDTs are now used in hundreds of millions per year.
source: Their swift adoption, now totaling hundreds of millions a year, coupled with effective artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) has led to significant progress in malaria control (Chiodini, 2014; Poti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chiodini 2014 and Poti et al. 2020

claim: The predominant falciparum malaria RDTs detect PfHRP2 and its paralog PfHRP3 due to cross-reactivity.
source: The predominant and most sensitive falciparum malaria RDTs detect PfHRP2 and, to a lesser extent, its paralog PfHRP3 due to cross-reactivity.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about RDT mechanisms

claim: Laboratory and field isolates with deletions of pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 have been reported in subtelomeric regions of chromosomes 8 and 13.
source: Unfortunately, a growing number of studies have reported laboratory and field isolates with deletions of pfhrp2 (PF3D7_0831800) and pfhrp3 (PF3D7_1372200) in the subtelomeric regions of chromosomes 8 and 13, respectively.
evidence: Supported by reference to multiple studies

claim: Parasites lacking PfHRP2 and PfHRP3 proteins can fully escape diagnosis by PfHRP2-based RDTs.
source: The resulting lack of these proteins allows the parasite to fully escape diagnosis by PfHRP2-based RDTs (Baker et al., 2005; Cheng et al., 2014; Organization WH, 2011; Poti et al., 2020; Thomson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Pfhrp2/3-deleted parasites appear to be spreading rapidly in some regions.
source: Pfhrp2/3-deleted parasites appear to be spreading rapidly in some regions and have compromised existing test-and-treat programs, especially in the Horn of Africa (Berhane et al., 2018; Feleke et al., 2021; Verma et al., 2018; WHO, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Pfhrp2/3-deleted parasites have compromised existing test-and-treat programs, especially in the Horn of Africa.
source: Pfhrp2/3-deleted parasites appear to be spreading rapidly in some regions and have compromised existing test-and-treat programs, especially in the Horn of Africa (Berhane et al., 2018; Feleke et al., 2021; Verma et al., 2018; WHO, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The prevalence of parasites with pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletion varies markedly across continents and regions in a manner not explained by RDT use alone.
source: The prevalence of parasites with pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletion varies markedly across continents and regions in a manner not explained by RDT use alone.
evidence: Supported by inference from observed patterns

claim: Parasites with pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions are well-established in areas where PfHRP2-based RDTs have never been used routinely, such as parts of South America.
source: Parasites with these deletions are well-established in areas where PfHRP2-based RDTs have never been used routinely, such as parts of South America (Thomson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomson et al. 2020

claim: In Ethiopia, the pfhrp3 deletion arose first, given it is more prevalent and shows a shorter shared haplotype.
source: Studies in Ethiopia, where false-negative RDTs owing to pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions are common, suggest that the pfhrp3 deletion arose first, given it is more prevalent and shows a shorter shared haplotype (Feleke et al., 2021).

claim: A 1994 study of the HB3 laboratory strain reported frequent meiotic translocation of a pfhrp3 deletion from chromosomes 13 to 11.
source: A 1994 study of the HB3 laboratory strain reported frequent meiotic translocation of a pfhrp3 deletion from chromosomes 13 to 11 (Hinterberg et al., 1994).

claim: Studies of P. falciparum structural rearrangements are challenging.
source: Studies of P. falciparum structural rearrangements are challenging, and pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions are particularly difficult due to their position in complex subtelomeric regions.

claim: Pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions are particularly difficult to study due to their position in complex subtelomeric regions.
source: Studies of P. falciparum structural rearrangements are challenging, and pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions are particularly difficult due to their position in complex subtelomeric regions.

claim: Subtelomeric regions represent roughly 5% of the P. falciparum genome.
source: Subtelomeric regions represent roughly 5% of the genome, are unstable, and contain rapidly diversifying gene families (e.g. var, rifin, stevor) that undergo frequent conversion between chromosomes mediated by non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) and double-stranded breakage (DSB) and telomere healing (Calhoun et al., 2017; Gardner et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2014; Mattei and Scherf, 1994; Reed et al., 2021; Vernick and McCutchan, 1988; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Subtelomeric regions are unstable and contain rapidly diversifying gene families.
source: Subtelomeric regions represent roughly 5% of the genome, are unstable, and contain rapidly diversifying gene families (e.g. var, rifin, stevor) that undergo frequent conversion between chromosomes mediated by non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) and double-stranded breakage (DSB) and telomere healing (Calhoun et al., 2017; Gardner et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2014; Mattei and Scherf, 1994; Reed et al., 2021; Vernick and McCutchan, 1988; Zhang et al., 2019).

claim: Subtelomeric gene families undergo frequent conversion between chromosomes mediated by non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) and double-stranded breakage (DSB) and telomere healing.

claim: Subtelomeric exchange allows for unbalanced progeny without the usual deleterious ramifications of altering a larger proportion of a chromosome.
source: Subtelomeric exchange importantly allows for unbalanced progeny without the usual deleterious ramifications of altering a larger proportion of a chromosome.

claim: Newly formed duplications predispose to further duplications or other rearrangements through NAHR between highly identical paralogous regions.

claim: Duplications potentiate the rapid expansion of gene families and their spread across subtelomeric regions.

source: The duplicative transposition of a subtelomeric region of one chromosome onto another chromosome frequently occurs in P. falciparum.

claim: Pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 are adjacent to but not considered part of the subtelomeric regions.
source: Notably, pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 are adjacent to but not considered part of the subtelomeric regions, and recombination of var genes does not result in the deletion of pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 (Feleke et al., 2021; Otto et al., 2018a).

claim: Recombination of var genes does not result in the deletion of pfhrp2 and pfhrp3.
source: Notably, pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 are adjacent to but not considered part of the subtelomeric regions, and recombination of var genes does not result in the deletion of pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 (Feleke et al., 2021; Otto et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feleke et al. 2021 and Otto et al. 2018a

claim: Telomere healing is de novo telomere addition via telomerase activity.
source: Telomere healing, de novo telomere addition via telomerase activity, is associated with subtelomeric deletion events in P. falciparum that involve chromosomal breakage and loss of all downstream genes.

claim: Telomere healing is associated with subtelomeric deletion events in P. falciparum that involve chromosomal breakage and loss of all downstream genes.
source: Telomere healing, de novo telomere addition via telomerase activity, is associated with subtelomeric deletion events in P. falciparum that involve chromosomal breakage and loss of all downstream genes.

claim: Healing serves to stabilize the end of the chromosome.
source: Healing serves to stabilize the end of the chromosome.

claim: Deletion of KAHRP and pfhrp2 genes via telomere healing was first reported to occur in laboratory isolates.

claim: Studies have defined the critical role of telomerase in P. falciparum and additional occurrences affecting several genes, including pfhrp1, Pf332, and Pf87 in laboratory isolates.

claim: The study examined all publicly available Illumina whole-genome sequencing data from global P. falciparum isolates as of January 2023, comprising 19,313 field samples and lab isolates.
source: We examined all publicly available Illumina whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from global P. falciparum isolates as of January 2023, comprising 19,313 field samples and lab isolates (Supplementary file 1).

claim: 3321 samples were eliminated from analysis, leaving 15,992 samples for further analysis.
source: This resulted in 3321 samples being eliminated, leaving 15,992 samples for further analysis.
evidence: Supported by data described in the manuscript

claim: The study identified 26 parasites with pfhrp2 deletion and 168 with pfhrp3 deletion.
source: We identified 26 parasites with pfhrp2 deletion and 168 with pfhrp3 deletion.

claim: Across all regions, pfhrp3 deletions were more common than pfhrp2 deletions.

claim: Twelve parasites with pfhrp2 deletion showed evidence of breakage and telomeric healing as suggested by TARE1 sequence contiguous with the genomic sequence at locations where coverage drops to zero.

claim: Most pfhrp2 deletion breakpoints occur within pfhrp2, found in 9 South American parasites and lab isolate D10.
source: Most breakpoints occur within pfhrp2, found in 9 South American parasites and lab isolate D10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Pfhrp2 deletion likely occurs solely through breakage events with subsequent telomeric healing.
source: Thus, pfhrp2 deletion likely occurs solely through breakage events with subsequent telomeric healing.

claim: Three distinct deletion copy number patterns are associated with pfhrp3 deletion.

source: Among the 168 parasites with pfhrp3 deletion, 20 (11.9%) were pattern 13-TARE1, 28 (16.6%) were pattern 13-5++, and the majority with 120 (71.4%) demonstrated pattern 13-11++.

claim: Pattern 13-11++ was almost exclusively found in parasites from Africa and the Americas, with six in Asia.
source: Pattern 13-11++ was almost exclusively found in parasites from Africa (n=39) and the Americas (n=75), with six in Asia, while 13-5++ was only observed in Asia (Figure 1).

claim: Pattern 13-5++ was only observed in Asia.
source: Pattern 13-11++ was almost exclusively found in parasites from Africa (n=39) and the Americas (n=75), with six in Asia, while 13-5++ was only observed in Asia (Figure 1).

claim: The 20 parasites with pattern 13-TARE1 had deletions of the core genome averaging 19 kb (range: 11–31 kb).

evidence: Supported by data and figure from the study

claim: The 28 parasites with deletion pattern 13-5++ had a consistent loss of 17.9 kb of chromosome 13 and a gain of 25 kb from chromosome 5.
source: The 28 parasites with deletion pattern 13-5++ had a consistent loss of 17.9 kb of chromosome 13 and a gain of 25 kb from chromosome 5.
evidence: Supported by data from the study

claim: Pattern 13-5++ isolates have evidence of a genomic rearrangement involving a 26 bp AT di-nucleotide repeat at 2,835,587 on chromosome 13, and a 20 bp AT di-nucleotide repeat at 979,203 on chromosome 5.
source: These isolates have evidence of a genomic rearrangement that involves a 26 bp AT di-nucleotide repeat at 2,835,587 on chromosome 13, and a 20 bp AT di-nucleotide repeat at 979,203 on chromosome 5.

claim: The 25 kb duplication in pattern 13-5++ contained several genes, including intact pfmdr1.
source: This 25 kb duplication contained several genes, including intact PF3D7_0523000 (pfmdr1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 5)

claim: Pattern 13-11++ was observed in 75 American parasites, 39 African parasites, and 6 Asian parasites.
source: Pattern 13-11++ was observed in 75 American parasites, 39 African parasites, and 6 Asian parasites (Figure 1).

claim: Of the 120 parasites with pattern 13-11++, 96 had near-identical copies of the chromosome 11 duplicated region.

claim: The 96 parasites containing identical copies of chromosome 11 duplicated region showed nine major haplotypes found in more than one sample and 14 haplotypes found only in one sample each.

claim: The different haplotypes showed geographical separation, with distinct haplotypes observed in American and African strains.

claim: The 15.2 kb segmental duplication was the largest duplication in the core genome based on an all-by-all unique k-mer genome comparison using nucmer.

claim: The two copies of the segmental duplication on chromosome 11 and chromosome 13 in the reference genome were 99.0% identical.

source: Each copy contained a centromeric 7 kb region encoding 2–3 undefined protein products (98.9% identity) and a telomeric 8 kb nearly identical region (99.7% identity) containing one of the two S-type (Gardner et al., 2002) ribosomal genes (S=sporozoite), which are primary expressed during life cycle stages in mosquito vector (Figure 3).

claim: No consistent nucleotide differences were found between the paralogs of the segmental duplication, leading to no distinct separation between copies when clustered.
source: No consistent nucleotide differences were found between the paralogs, leading to no distinct separation between copies when clustered (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data and figure from the study

claim: The lack of consistent nucleotide differences between paralogs suggests ongoing interchromosomal exchanges or conversion events maintaining paralog homogeneity.
source: This suggests ongoing interchromosomal exchanges or conversion events maintaining paralog homogeneity.

claim: The Plasmodium praefalciparum genome contained similar S-type rRNA loci on chromosomes 11 and 13 and had a similar gene synteny to P. falciparum in these regions.
source: The Plasmodium praefalciparum genome, which is P. falciparum's closest relative, having diverged about 50,000 years ago (Otto et al., 2018b), also contained similar S-type rRNA loci on chromosomes 11 and 13 and had a similar gene synteny to P. falciparum in these regions and the region on chromosome 8 neighboring pfhrp2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

source: The contig matching the hybrid 13–11 for both strains essentially contained a duplicated portion of chromosome 11 telomeric to the ribosomal duplication.
evidence: Supported by data from the study

claim: The duplicated genes within the chromosome 11 segment included pf332, two ring erythrocyte surface antigens genes, three PHISTs genes, a FIKK family gene, and two hypothetical proteins, and ends with a DnaJ gene.
source: The duplicated genes within this segment included pf332 (PF3D7_1149000), two ring erythrocyte surface antigens genes (PF3D7_1149200, PF3D7_1149500), three PHISTs genes, a FIKK family gene, and two hypothetical proteins, and ends with a DnaJ gene (PF3D7_1149600) corresponding to 3D7 genes PF3D7_1148700 through PF3D7_1149600 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
